concepts.title: Herbivores, Carnivores and Omnivores
concepts.explanation:
You can already build a food chain and name the producer and the consumers in it. Now sort the consumers, because they are not all doing the same job.

A herbivore eats only plants. A goat, a cow, a zebra and a grasshopper are herbivores. Look at their teeth and you find wide, flat grinders and no tearing teeth, because grass and leaves have to be ground down rather than torn.

A carnivore eats only other animals. A lion, a hawk, a crocodile and a spider are carnivores. Their teeth are pointed for holding and tearing, and their eyes usually face forwards, which helps in judging the distance to something they are chasing.

An omnivore eats both plants and animals. A chicken, a pig, a crow and a human being are omnivores. That is why your mouth has flat grinders at the back AND pointed teeth at the front - you are built for both kinds of food.

Now put the words together with the chain. In grass → goat → lion, the grass is the producer, the goat is a herbivore, and the lion is a carnivore. The animal that eats another is the predator; the one eaten is the prey. A single animal can be both - a snake preys on a rat and is itself prey to a hawk.

A food chain therefore tells you two things at once: which way the food travels, and what kind of eater each link is.
concepts.example: Write a food chain with four links from a habitat near you. Label each consumer as a herbivore, a carnivore or an omnivore, and say which pair in your chain are predator and prey.

concepts.title: Keeping a Body Healthy
concepts.explanation:
Living things need food, water and air. Staying healthy takes three more things, and each one has real science behind it.

MOVEMENT. A body that moves works better. When you run, your heart beats faster and pushes blood round more quickly, and your breathing deepens to take in more oxygen. Do that regularly and the heart muscle itself grows stronger, so it can move the same blood with fewer beats. Movement also keeps bones strong and joints working freely, and it helps you sleep. Sitting still all day does the opposite: the muscles weaken, and the heart never gets asked to do anything difficult.

MEDICINES. Some illnesses will not pass on their own, and a medicine can treat them. A medicine is a carefully measured substance that changes something inside the body, which is exactly why it must be used correctly: the right medicine, the amount written on it, at the times given, and only the one prescribed for the person who is ill. Taking somebody else's medicine, or taking more than the amount, can do serious harm - the same substance that treats an illness in the right amount is dangerous in the wrong one. Medicines are kept away from small children and are only ever given by an adult.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE. Some illnesses spread from one living thing to another - measles, flu and cholera in people, and diseases in plants and farm animals too. Those are called infectious. Washing hands, covering a cough and drinking clean water all cut down the spreading.

And some infectious diseases can be stopped before they start. A vaccination teaches the body to recognise one particular disease, so that if it ever meets the real thing the body is ready to fight it off. That is why children are vaccinated against measles and polio - not to treat an illness they have, but to prevent one they might otherwise catch.
concepts.example: Name one thing you did today that was good for your heart. Then explain the difference between a medicine and a vaccination: which one treats an illness you already have, and which one prevents one you have not caught?

concepts.title: Changes That Cannot Be Undone
concepts.explanation:
Melting, freezing, boiling and dissolving all have something in common: you can get back what you started with. Freeze the water again and you have the ice cube. Let the salty water dry and the salt is still there.

There is another kind of change, and it works only one way.

Burn a piece of paper. Grey ash and smoke are left. You cannot cool the ash and get paper. The paper reacted with the oxygen in the air, and the ash and smoke are NEW substances - not paper in a new shape or a new state, but different materials altogether.

Bake a cake and the batter becomes cake. Fry an egg and the clear part turns white and solid, and no amount of cooling makes it clear again. Leave an iron nail out in the rain and a crumbly orange layer grows on it: rust, a new substance made from iron, water and oxygen.

When substances react to make one or more new substances, the change cannot be reversed. We call it an irreversible change.

That reacting together has its own name too: it is called a chemical reaction. Burning paper, rusting iron and baking a cake are all chemical reactions, because in each one the starting substances react and turn into different substances - not the same stuff in a new shape, but new stuff altogether.

There are signs to watch for. A new colour appearing. Bubbles of gas when nothing is boiling. Heat or light given out. A smell that was not there before. Any of those is a hint that something new has been made rather than merely moved or melted.

So the test is not whether the change looks big. It is whether you still have the same substances. Ice and water are the same substance in two states; paper and ash are two different substances, and that is why one change goes back and the other does not.
concepts.example: Sort these into reversible and irreversible: melting butter, burning charcoal, dissolving sugar, an egg frying, water boiling, a nail rusting. For each irreversible one, name the sign that told you a new substance had been made.

concepts.title: The Earth in Space
concepts.explanation:
You have looked at the Earth from the inside - crust, mantle and core. Now step back and look at it from the outside.

WHY WE HAVE DAY AND NIGHT. The Earth spins, like a ball turning on a rod through it. That rod is called its axis, and one whole turn takes twenty-four hours. Sunlight falls on whichever half is facing the Sun; the other half is in shadow. Where you are standing it is day, then the Earth turns you away and it is night. The Sun looks as though it crosses the sky from east to west, but the Sun is not the thing moving - you are, along with the ground you are standing on. That is why sunrise and sunset happen at all.

THE SUN IS AT THE CENTRE. The Sun is a star, and it sits at the centre of everything near us. The Earth travels round the Sun once a year, held by gravity, and it is not alone.

THE PLANETS. Eight planets travel round the Sun. In order from the Sun outwards they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four are small and rocky, like ours. The next four are enormous and made mostly of gas - Jupiter is so big that more than a thousand Earths would fit inside it. The further out a planet is, the longer its year: Mercury goes round in 88 days, while Neptune takes 165 of our years.

WHAT ELSE IS OUT THERE. A system like this holds more than a star and its planets. There are asteroids - lumps of rock, most of them in a wide belt between Mars and Jupiter. There are comets - balls of ice and dust on long journeys, growing a bright tail when they come close to the Sun and the ice turns to gas. Moons circle many of the planets, and ours is one of them.

So the Sun is one star with a family around it, and ours is not the only such family. Other stars have planets of their own.
concepts.example: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun. Then explain, without using the word 'sunrise', why the Sun appears to move across your sky - and say what is really moving.
